name: Carrion-Deep
description: Carrion-Deep earned its grim name from the fossilized forests that cover its equatorial regions, billions of petrified trees standing exactly as they died in some ancient cataclysm. The canyon systems cut through these stone forests, revealing cross-sections of an ecosystem frozen in death—root systems, fungal networks, even the preserved impressions of creatures caught mid-stride. Beneath this museum of extinction, a liquid ocean somehow survives, warmed by geological processes that have outlasted the surface biosphere by millions of years.

The thin atmosphere carries a faint organic scent near the canyon vents, where gases from the deep ocean reach the surface. This smell—somewhere between sulfur and decay—earned the planet its name before surveys revealed its source. The petrified forests creak and groan with thermal expansion, a sound disconcertingly like footsteps to those walking among the stone trunks. Shadows fall at odd angles through the fossilized canopy, creating patterns that sometimes seem almost deliberate.

Life persists in the deep ocean, extremophile bacteria that have evolved in isolation for longer than complex life has existed on Earth. These organisms produce compounds found nowhere else, molecules with proven applications in medicine and biotechnology. The research outpost established to study them has operated for fifteen years, its staff rotating through six-month shifts in conditions that test psychological endurance.

The quarantine zone surrounding the primary research site exists because of an incident no official report fully explains. Something in the deep samples affected three researchers in ways that required their permanent isolation. They're still alive, technically, but they no longer communicate in any recognized language. The research continues despite—or perhaps because of—this mystery, the potential benefits too significant to abandon. The ocean holds secrets worth fortunes, and perhaps costs that haven't yet been fully calculated.
